newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung defends China's plan to dilute rights.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung defends China's plan to dilute rights.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa on Friday defended Beijing's plans to roll back the territory's human rights and civil liberties laws after it resumes sovereignty of the British colony.
"It is not a roll-back on civil liberty, it is really an issue of balancing between rights and order of our society," Tung said in an interview with CNN broadcast on Friday.

Hong Kong, a British colony of over 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 and the territory is jittery over whether its freewheeling and democratic ways will be allowed to continue as guaranteed in the Joint Declaration.
The 1984 treaty outlines the terms of Hong Kong's return to China.
China's parliament last Sunday approved a plan to throw out or amend a clutch of Hong Kong laws -- including those that provide for democratic elections and protect civil liberties.
The plan dilutes Hong Kong's bill of rights, the law on forming political parties and another on free association that takes a liberal approach to public protests and demonstrations.
But Tung was adamant that these imminent changes were not tantamount to eroding civil liberties.
"It is not a question about civil liberties," he said.

While Tung said he was confident Beijing was committed to allowing Hong Kong a high degree of self-rule after the handover, he hinted that people in territory would not be allowed to make slanderous or derogatory remarks about Chinese leaders.
He said any such limits which may be introduced would merely be an extension of existing laws.
"Under today's law, it is unlawful to make slanderous or derogatory remarks against the royal family," he said.
"Now if this law is adapted, and I say "if" because it is now being looked at, and if this law is adapted, then to make similar remarks against Chinese leaders would be unlawful."
Hong Kong's chief executive, as Tung will be known after the handover, also said bread-and-butter issues among Hong Kong's 6.3 million people overrode their concerns about political liberties.
"We have a spiralling cost of housing ... mismatch of skills, education ... these are the real problems which people care about," he said.
